title: Where to Start with Amsterdam's Golden Age
dek: Eight books on how one city came to dominate trade

slides.heading: Start with the Culture of Wealth
slides.body: Simon Schama, *The Embarrassment of Riches* (1987). It shows how the Dutch lived with sudden prosperity: moral unease, cleanliness, display. Its interpretation is debated, but it is the most readable door into the period.

slides.heading: Then the Share Market
slides.body: Lodewijk Petram, *The World's First Stock Exchange* (2014, English edition). VOC shares traded from 1602, followed by forwards and short selling. The title's claim is contested: Antwerp had an exchange earlier, though not for company shares.

art.title: Interior of the Oude Kerk, Delft

slides.heading: The Global Reach
slides.body: C. R. Boxer, *The Dutch Seaborne Empire, 1600 to 1800* (1965). It is an older classic, and still the clearest single account of how the VOC and WIC carried Amsterdam's capital across the Indian Ocean and Atlantic.

slides.heading: The City as Money Market
slides.body: Violet Barbour, *Capitalism in Amsterdam in the Seventeenth Century* (1950). It is short and archival. Barbour traces the commodity trade, the Exchange Bank founded in 1609, and the lending that made Amsterdam Europe's capital market.

art.title: The Council Chamber in Amsterdam Town Hall

slides.heading: Braudel's World-Economy
slides.body: Fernand Braudel, *The Perspective of the World* (1979), volume three of *Civilization and Capitalism*. Braudel treats Amsterdam as the last city to stand at the centre of a world-economy before London and national economies took over.

art.title: The Y at Amsterdam, with the Frigate 'De Ploeg

slides.heading: The Primacy Thesis
slides.body: Jonathan Israel, *Dutch Primacy in World Trade, 1585 to 1740* (1989). Israel argues that dominance rested on high-value rich trades and the Amsterdam staple market, not only the Baltic bulk trade. That emphasis remains contested.
slides.art_query: Willem van de Velde Dutch merchant ships

art.title: A Dutch Flagship and a Fluyt Running into a Mediterranean Harbour

slides.heading: The Long Economic Arc
slides.body: Jan de Vries and Ad van der Woude, *The First Modern Economy* (1997). This is the standard synthesis on growth, energy, agriculture and decline from 1500 to 1815. Its central claim, the Dutch economy as the first modern one, is debated.
slides.source: De Vries and Van der Woude 1997
slides.art_query: Ruisdael Windmill at Wijk bij Duurstede

art.title: De molen bij Wijk bij Duurstede The Windmill at Wijk bij Duurstede

slides.heading: Finish with the Institutions
slides.body: Oscar Gelderblom, *Cities of Commerce* (2013). Comparing Bruges, Antwerp and Amsterdam from 1250 to 1650, he argues that commercial institutions improved through competition between cities, not through any single superior design.

art.title: Market scene with baskets and historic buildings
art.artist: Photo by Art Institute of Chicago

caption:
Amsterdam's dominance had no single cause, and the eight books below disagree about which ones mattered most.
Israel puts the weight on rich trades and the staple market (Israel 1989). De Vries and Van der Woude call the Republic the first modern economy (De Vries and Van der Woude 1997). Gelderblom credits competition between cities (Gelderblom 2013). Read them in order and the argument comes into focus.

risk_notes: Petram's title 'first stock exchange': Antwerp had an exchange earlier, so the slide is flagged. Defend with 'the first sustained secondary market in company shares'.
Israel's rich-trades thesis is challenged by scholars who stress the Baltic bulk trade as the 'mother trade'. The slide is flagged as contested.
Whether the 'first modern economy' label holds is debated. The slide attributes it to De Vries and Van der Woude and flags it.
Schama's cultural reading has been criticised as impressionistic. The slide notes that his interpretation is debated.
Braudel dates: French original 1979, English translation 1984. If challenged, cite both.
Boxer and Israel subtitles use date ranges written with 'to' to avoid dashes. The original titles use a dash.

issues.problem: "The Perspective of the World* (1979)" gives the English title with the date of the French original (*Le Temps du monde*, 1979). The English translation came out in 1984. The risk note mentions this, but the slide itself mixes the two editions.
issues.fix: Write "Fernand Braudel, *The Perspective of the World* (1979; English 1984), volume three of *Civilization and Capitalism*." This keeps the body within 40 words. Alternatively, write "(1984, English edition)" to match the Petram slide.

issues.problem: "De Vries and Van der Woude call the Republic the first modern economy" states the label without the caveat that slide 7 gives it. A reader who only sees the caption won't know it's debated.
issues.fix: Change it to "De Vries and Van der Woude make the debated case that the Republic was the first modern economy (De Vries and Van der Woude 1997)."
